title: THEY CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. THE BIBLE NEVER DID.
paragraphs: THEY CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. THE BIBLE NEVER DID.
For Centuries, a Woman Who Wept at Jesus’ Feet Has Carried a Reputation Scripture Never Gave Her. But What Jesus Said About Her Will Break Your Heart—and Might Change How You See Your Own Past.
“And he said to the woman, Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50 (KJV)
What if I told you that one of the most emotionally powerful encounters with Jesus Christ has been retold for centuries with an accusation the Bible itself never makes?
What if a woman remembered for her tears, her courage, and her extraordinary love for Jesus has also been remembered by a label Luke never placed upon her?

And what if the most heartbreaking part of her story is not what she had done before meeting Jesus, but how easily religious people can become more interested in someone's past than in the Savior standing right in front of them?
Because somewhere in this world, there is a woman who has spent years trying to outrun something she regrets.
There is a man who still believes his worst decision is his permanent identity.
There is someone sitting quietly in church, smiling through worship, while secretly wondering whether God could ever look at them without remembering everything they have done.
And perhaps, without telling anyone, that someone is you.
If so, please don't rush past this story.
There is a woman in Luke chapter 7 whom people have been discussing for nearly two thousand years.
We know she cried.
We know she carried an alabaster vessel of ointment.
We know she stood behind Jesus, washed His feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed His feet, and anointed them.
We know she was called a sinner.
But there is something we do not know.
The Bible never tells us that she was a prostitute.
Not once.
And that distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because when we add details God did not reveal, we risk turning someone's testimony into a story Scripture never actually told.
Luke 7:36–50 begins with an invitation.
A Pharisee named Simon asks Jesus to eat at his house.
Jesus accepts.
Picture the scene.

A meal is underway. Guests are reclining around the table according to the dining customs of the time. Conversations are taking place. Simon is hosting a Teacher whose reputation has already begun attracting attention.
And then someone enters who changes the entire atmosphere.
Luke 7:37 says:
“And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment.” (KJV)
Notice the language carefully.
Luke calls her a woman in the city who was a sinner.
The Greek text describes her as:
γυνὴ ... ἥτις ἦν ... ἁμαρτωλός
Transliterated: gynē ... hētis ēn ... hamartōlos.
A woman who was a sinner.
The word ἁμαρτωλός (hamartōlos) means “sinful” or “sinner.”
It does not, by itself, mean prostitute.
Greek had other vocabulary available for prostitution, including πόρνη (pornē), a word used elsewhere in the New Testament.
Luke does not use that word here.

This does not prove that the woman had never engaged in prostitution. It means that Scripture does not identify prostitution as her sin, and we have no biblical authority to present it as an established fact.
She may have been known publicly for serious moral wrongdoing. The narrative suggests that her reputation was familiar to people in the community.
But the nature of her wrongdoing is not disclosed.
That silence should make us careful.
Because there is a difference between what Scripture reveals and what tradition assumes.
And there is a difference between recognizing someone's sin and inventing the details of it.
For generations, the unnamed woman in Luke 7 has often been associated with Mary Magdalene, sometimes with Mary of Bethany, and frequently with the image of a repentant prostitute.

That association developed through later Christian interpretation, particularly in Western church tradition. Pope Gregory the Great's sermon in AD 591 famously helped popularize the identification of these women as one person.
But these are not identifications made by Luke 7 itself.
Mary Magdalene is introduced by name in Luke 8:2 as a woman from whom seven demons had gone out.
The passage does not identify her as a prostitute either.
And the account of Mary of Bethany anointing Jesus in John 12:1–8 occurs in a different narrative setting, involving a named woman, a meal in Bethany, and the approaching burial of Jesus.
There are similarities among the Gospel anointing accounts, and Christians have historically interpreted their relationships in different ways.
But similarities do not give us permission to erase distinctions.
We must not confuse later tradition with the actual wording of Scripture.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Imagine having your worst season become the only thing people remember about you.
Imagine people talking about your past without knowing your full story.
Imagine being reduced to a label while the most important thing that ever happened to you—your encounter with Jesus—is pushed into the background.
We do not know how this woman first came to hear about Christ.
We do not know what specific sins she had committed.
We do not know what conversations, disappointments, regrets, or moments of awakening brought her to Simon's house.
But Luke tells us what she did when she reached Jesus.

“And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.” — Luke 7:38 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
She was weeping.
Not delivering a polished speech.
Not defending her reputation.
Not presenting a carefully prepared explanation for her presence.
She was crying at the feet of Jesus.
The Greek verb translated “weeping,” κλαίουσα (klaiousa), comes from klaiō, meaning to weep or lament.
Luke describes tears so abundant that they wet His feet.
Then she wipes them with her hair.
She kisses His feet repeatedly.
She pours out the ointment she brought.
Every movement reveals an intensity of emotion that Simon's orderly dinner could never contain.
Her actions are extraordinary expressions of humility, affection, and devotion.
And perhaps that is why this scene remains so unforgettable.
Because some of the deepest encounters with God happen when a person no longer has beautiful words to offer.
Only tears.
Only surrender.
Only the desperate awareness that the One before them is worthy of everything.
Have you ever prayed like that?
Not the kind of prayer you could confidently say in front of a congregation.
Not a carefully worded prayer filled with familiar religious phrases.
But the kind whispered after another failure.
The kind that comes when you have disappointed yourself again.
When the same temptation has returned.
When you have promised God you would change, only to discover how weak you still are.
When all you can manage is:
“Jesus, please have mercy on me.”
If you have ever been there, you may understand something about this woman that Simon did not.
Because Simon saw her enter the room.
But he did not truly see her.
Luke 7:39 records his private reaction:
“This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner.” (KJV)
There it is.
Simon has already reached his conclusion.
He knows what kind of woman she is.
And because Jesus allows her to touch His feet, Simon begins questioning whether Jesus is really a prophet.
Think about that.
The woman is expressing extraordinary love.
Jesus is receiving her.
And Simon is silently judging them both.
The irony is devastating.
Simon doubts Jesus' prophetic knowledge because he assumes Jesus does not know the woman's reputation.
But Jesus immediately demonstrates that He knows something Simon has not spoken aloud.
His thoughts.
“Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee.” — Luke 7:40 (KJV)
And with those words, the entire dinner changes.
Jesus tells a story about two debtors.
One owes five hundred denarii.
The other owes fifty.
Neither can repay.
The lender freely forgives both debts.
Then Jesus asks Simon which debtor will love the lender more.
Simon answers that it would be the one forgiven more.
Jesus tells him he has judged correctly.
The Greek word describing the cancellation of the debts is related to χαρίζομαι (charizomai), meaning to give graciously, show favor, or forgive.
It is a beautiful word in this setting.
The debtors do not negotiate their way out.
They do not earn cancellation by performing enough good deeds.
They are unable to pay.
The creditor graciously releases them.
And that is the point Jesus wants Simon to understand.
Forgiveness is not a trophy awarded to people who have successfully repaired themselves. It is grace given to people who cannot pay their debt.
Then Jesus turns toward the woman.
But He speaks to Simon.
“Seest thou this woman?” — Luke 7:44 (KJV)
Five words.
And perhaps the most piercing question in the entire encounter.
Simon had already looked at her.
He had noticed her entrance.
He had recognized her reputation.
He had judged her presence.
But Jesus asks whether he actually sees her.
Not merely her reputation.
Not merely her sin.
Her.
The woman standing before him.
The person whose tears have fallen onto the feet of the Messiah.
The person whose love has become impossible to ignore.
Jesus continues by contrasting Simon's hospitality with the woman's actions.
Simon had given Him no water for His feet.
She had washed them with tears.
Simon had offered no customary greeting kiss.
She had not stopped kissing His feet.
Simon had not anointed His head with oil.
She had anointed His feet with ointment.
And suddenly the respected host is being confronted by the very Guest he invited.
Not because hospitality rituals could purchase salvation.
But because the woman's actions reveal a love and gratitude that Simon has failed to recognize.
Here is something we need to understand.
The woman is not presented as sinless.
Jesus never pretends that her wrongdoing was harmless.
He does not redefine evil as good.
He does not suggest repentance is unnecessary.
He acknowledges the seriousness of her sins.
But He also refuses to let her sins be the final word about her.
Listen to Luke 7:47:
“Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἀφέωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῆς (apheōntai hai hamartiai autēs) means “her sins have been forgiven.”
The verb apheōntai is in the perfect tense, presenting forgiveness as a completed reality with continuing significance.
This matters.
Jesus is not teaching that the woman purchased forgiveness with her tears, her perfume, or her affection.
His parable has already established that the debts were graciously canceled.
The love of the forgiven debtor flows from the forgiveness received.
And Luke 7:50 confirms the central point when Jesus declares that her faith has saved her.
Her actions reveal the reality of her faith and love.
They do not make her the purchaser of divine mercy.
Her tears were not the price of forgiveness. They were the overflow of a heart responding to grace.
And that is the Gospel.
We are not saved because we cry enough.
We are not saved because we have suffered enough.
We are not saved because we have successfully convinced God that our good deeds now outweigh our failures.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Salvation is God's gift.
It is received through faith.
And that saving grace is made possible through Jesus Christ—through His sinless life, His sacrificial death for sinners, and His victorious resurrection.
The woman at Simon's house did not yet stand on the far side of Calvary as we do when reading her story.
But the Savior who would give His life for sinners was already standing before her.
And He had authority to forgive sins.
When Jesus tells her that her sins are forgiven, the other guests begin asking:
“Who is this that forgiveth sins also?” — Luke 7:49 (KJV)
That is not a minor question.
It is the question that leads us to the heart of the entire passage.
Who is Jesus?
Is He merely a teacher with an unusually compassionate personality?
Is He simply a religious reformer willing to challenge social expectations?
Is He only an example of how to treat people whom society has rejected?
No.
He is far more.
He is the Christ, the Son of God, the Savior whose authority reaches beyond social shame into the deepest human need.
The forgiveness of sins.
And if we read this account only as a lesson about being less judgmental, we will miss the greatest miracle in the room.
A sinner came near to Jesus, and Jesus declared her forgiven.
That is the center of the story.
Not a scandalous occupation Luke never names.
Not an imagined biography.
Not even the perfume.
Jesus.
His authority.
His mercy.
His grace.
And the faith that receives His salvation.
There is a warning here for every believer, including those of us who love the Scriptures and defend biblical truth.
It is possible to know religious language while becoming dangerously comfortable with judging people.
It is possible to recognize sin accurately while failing to respond with humility and compassion.
It is possible to defend holiness while forgetting how desperately we ourselves depend on grace.
Simon was not wrong to believe sin mattered.
Sin does matter.
It destroys.
It deceives.
It separates people from the life God created them to enjoy.
And Jesus did not come to make sin respectable.
He came to save sinners.
But Simon's mistake was believing that the woman's known sin made her unworthy of approaching Jesus.
He saw her reputation as a reason for distance.
Jesus revealed that her faith had brought her to the very One who could forgive her.
And we need to ask ourselves an uncomfortable question.
How many people have we quietly written off because we knew something about their past?
The woman who became pregnant outside marriage.
The man whose marriage collapsed because of his unfaithfulness.
The recovering addict who still struggles.
The former prisoner trying to rebuild his life.
The believer who fell publicly and now fears returning to church.
The person whose sins are visible while ours remain carefully concealed.
We must never call sin righteousness.
But neither should we treat another person's failure as proof that God's mercy cannot reach them.
The same Christ who commands repentance also welcomes repentant sinners.
And none of us stands before God on the strength of a spotless personal history.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
All.
Not merely the people whose failures became public.
Not merely those whose sins offend our personal sensibilities.
All of us.
And if you have been forgiven by Christ, you have no reason to boast over someone still struggling to find their way to Him.
You have every reason to point them toward the Savior.
Perhaps that is why this passage is so powerful.
Because we are tempted to decide which person in the room we resemble.
We imagine ourselves as the woman because we know what shame feels like.
Or we imagine ourselves as Simon because we recognize the danger of religious pride.
But the truth is that many of us have been both.
We have been the sinner desperate for mercy.
And we have been the religious observer too quick to condemn.
We have cried over our own failures.
And then, somehow, forgotten those tears when confronted with someone else's.
We have begged God to be patient with our weaknesses.
And then expected another person to change overnight.
We have celebrated forgiveness when it was offered to us.
And questioned it when it was offered to someone we disliked.
That is a painful confession.
But spiritual maturity begins when we allow Scripture to examine us instead of using Scripture only to examine everybody else.
Maybe you need to hear this today.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame is not beyond His mercy.
Your sins are not too deeply buried for Him to expose and forgive.
But His grace is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
To confess what you have been hiding.
To turn from the sin that has been destroying you.
To trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And to begin walking in the newness of life that only He can give.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Broken trust may take time to rebuild.
Wounded relationships may require patient repair.
Some consequences may remain even after genuine repentance.
But forgiveness in Christ is real.
And a person who belongs to Jesus is not required to spend the rest of their life pretending that grace has no power to transform them.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to deny what happened.
It is the announcement that what happened does not have to define the whole future.
And this brings us back to the unnamed woman.
We do not know her name.
We do not know her occupation.
We do not know the complete story of her sins.
We do not know what became of her in the years after that dinner.
Scripture does not tell us.
But it does preserve the words Jesus spoke to her.
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50 (KJV)
In Greek:
Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
The word σέσωκέν (sesōken) comes from sōzō, meaning to save, rescue, or deliver.
And εἰρήνη (eirēnē) means peace.
The expression “go in peace” is more than a casual farewell in this context.
It is spoken by the very One who has just declared her forgiven and affirmed her saving faith.
Imagine what it meant to hear those words.
She entered a house where at least one man saw her primarily through the lens of her sins.
She encountered Jesus.
And the last words Luke records Him speaking to her were not a rehearsal of her failures.
They were an affirmation of salvation and a command to depart in peace.
Do you see the contrast?
Simon was occupied with what kind of sinner she had been.
Jesus spoke about what faith had received.
Simon looked backward at her reputation.
Jesus announced forgiveness and sent her forward in peace.
And that is why we must stop pretending that the most important detail about this woman is an occupation the Bible never assigns to her.
The story is not about proving that her sins were small.
Jesus explicitly says they were many.
It is about discovering that the mercy of Christ is greater than the sins of those who come to Him in faith.
Somebody reading this has been living as though the courtroom is still in session even after coming to Christ.
You keep reopening the case.
You keep presenting the evidence against yourself.
You keep replaying conversations, decisions, betrayals, addictions, compromises, and failures.
You remember things that happened ten years ago as though they happened this morning.
And every time you begin to experience peace, a familiar voice whispers:
“You know what you did.”
Yes.
God knows too.
And the Gospel does not ask you to pretend otherwise.
It calls you to trust the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because justice no longer matters.
But because Christ has borne the judgment due to sinners, and those united to Him by faith are no longer under condemnation.
This is not cheap grace.
It cost the Son of God His life.
And it calls those who receive it into a life of repentance, obedience, gratitude, and love.
So if you are still hiding from Jesus because you believe your past makes you untouchable, consider the woman at His feet.
And if you are still standing at a distance, convinced that another person's sins make them beyond redemption, consider Simon.
Then look beyond them both.
Look at Christ.
Because neither the woman's tears nor Simon's respectability is the foundation of salvation.
Jesus is.
And maybe today, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop trying to impress God with the appearance of being okay.
Come honestly.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Seek reconciliation where you have caused harm.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And allow His Word to reshape the way you see yourself and others.
And if this passage challenged the way you have judged people, perhaps your response can be even simpler:
“Lord, teach me to see people as You see them.”

I hope the comments beneath this article become more than reactions. I hope they become a place where believers pray for one another, where repentance is taken seriously, where testimonies point to Jesus, and where struggling souls are reminded that the Gospel is still good news.
Because someone else needs to hear this.
Someone whose reputation has followed them into every new season of life.
Someone who thinks church is only for people with clean histories.
Someone who has been told that their mistakes make them permanently unworthy.
Not because a page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But faithful biblical teaching can continually direct people to the Savior, strengthen believers in truth, challenge complacency, and encourage hearts that are growing weary.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.

We want to keep bringing Scripture into ordinary lives, into difficult conversations, into homes where people are struggling silently, and into the daily decisions where faith is either lived or forgotten.
These resources are intended to help people study the Bible, understand the Gospel, develop spiritual discipline, and become more firmly rooted in Christ.
The Bible teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not forced by guilt or fear.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These are simple items, but they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, thoughtful gifts, and practical resources for everyday Christian living.
Pray for the ministry.
Use the free resources.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Every sincere act of support matters, and none should be confused with the free gift of salvation.
But before you leave, I want to return to one final detail.
The woman in Luke 7 never receives a name in this account.
Her personal history remains largely unknown.
Her particular sins are never itemized.
Her occupation is never revealed.
And yet, nearly two thousand years later, we are still reading about the moment she encountered Jesus.
Isn't that extraordinary?
The world wants to know what she did.
Jesus wants Simon to understand what forgiveness has produced.
The world keeps searching for the scandal.
Luke directs our attention to the Savior.
And the final word spoken to this woman in the passage is not “sinner.”
It is peace.
That does not mean her past never happened.
It means her past was not the end of her story.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, neither is yours.
So do not add accusations where Scripture is silent.
Do not minimize sin where Scripture speaks plainly.
Do not withhold compassion where Christ demonstrates mercy.
And never allow the failures of a human being to eclipse the glory of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
Because the most unforgettable truth about the woman who anointed Jesus is not what people have called her.
It is what Jesus said to her.
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.”
And perhaps the words your wounded heart needs to remember tonight are these:
The world may keep calling you by the name of your worst chapter, but in Christ, your worst chapter does not get to write your final sentence.
